Same agency, different presentations, different filing positions. The exam may test this awareness by presenting the same agency in different forms across questions, or by placing an acronym and its full name in the same mixed list (rare but possible).

The government office rule is the most complex TANG rule because it requires genuine rearrangement (unlike company-as-written or acronym-as-written) and correct identification of the distinctive element (unlike number conversion which is more mechanical). It's also the rule most often violated under exam pressure because filing 'Department of Education' under D feels natural — overriding this instinct with the E-filing rule requires trained discipline.

SIMPLIFIED: CSE Sub-Professional (165 items, 2h40m, 80% passing) — government office questions are the hardest business filing items.
The exam's #1 trap: filing departments under D instead of their distinctive word.
Common distractor: an answer with all departments clustered together. That's wrong — they should spread out.
Read question instructions! If it says 'file as written,' government offices DON'T get rearranged.
Sub-Professional Clerical Ability always includes at least one government office in mixed lists.
STANDARD: In the CSE Sub-Professional (165 items, 2h40m, 80% passing), government office questions are the highest-difficulty business filing items. The distinctive-word rule requires rearrangement that feels unnatural, and the exam exploits this by including distractors where departments cluster under D.

CSE exam pattern (Sub-Professional, 165 items, 2h40m, 80% to pass): A distractor answer will have 'Department of...' entries grouped together (all under D). If you see this clustering in an answer choice, it's almost certainly wrong — the distinctive-word rule distributes them.

For the CSE Sub-Professional (165 items, 2h40m, 80% passing), the most common government filing scenario: 3-5 departments in the same list. You must identify each distinctive word and scatter them across the alphabet. Budget(B), Education(E), Health(H), Justice(J), Labor(L) — all different sections.

CSE strategy (Sub-Professional, 165 items, 2h40m, 80% passing): For government offices, mentally cross out 'Department of' / 'Bureau of' and read only the remaining word(s). That remainder tells you the filing section. This mental deletion is faster than formal rearrangement.

Critical CSE instruction awareness (Sub-Professional, 165 items, 2h40m, 80% passing): Some questions state 'file all entries exactly as written.' When this instruction appears, government offices file under their FIRST word (Department→D, Bureau→B). Override your default distinctive-word rule when explicitly instructed. Read instructions FIRST.
DETAILED: The CSE Sub-Professional (165 items, 2h40m, 80% passing) uses government office entries as the primary differentiator in business filing questions. Most examinees handle company names and acronyms correctly — it's the government office rule that separates passing from failing. The exam designs questions where getting the government entry wrong cascades into selecting the wrong answer choice (because one entry in the wrong position changes the entire sequence).

Exam distractor construction for CSE Sub-Professional (165 items, 2h40m, 80% to pass): In a 5-entry mixed list, one distractor places the government office under its generic word (D for Department). Another distractor places it correctly but orders the other entries wrong. The correct answer applies ALL TANG rules correctly to ALL entries. Government office misplacement is the single most common error that distractors exploit.

For the CSE Sub-Professional (165 items, 2h40m, 80% passing): The exam occasionally tests the 'instruction override' scenario. If instructions say 'arrange the following entries alphabetically,' use the CSE default (distinctive word first). If instructions say 'file all entries exactly as they are written,' file Department under D. This instruction sensitivity tests reading comprehension alongside filing knowledge.

Strategic time allocation for CSE Sub-Professional (165 items, 2h40m, 80% passing): Government office entries take the most processing time in mixed lists. Budget 5-8 seconds per government entry (identify → strip prefix → determine distinctive word → note first letter). Compare with companies (2 seconds) and acronyms (1 second). Allocate your item time budget accordingly.

For the CSE Sub-Professional Clerical Ability section (165 items, 2h40m, 80% passing): Government office questions have the highest 'rule knowledge premium' — knowing the distinctive-word rule is both necessary and sufficient for correct answers. Without it, you'll guess wrong. With it, the answer is deterministic. This makes government filing the single highest-ROI study target within business filing: learn one rule, earn points on every question that includes a government office entry.

SIMPLIFIED: Ask: 'Department of WHAT?' The answer is where you file. Education→E, Health→H, Budget→B.
TANG rule G: Government = distinctive word first. Drop the prefix, keep the key word.
Mental trick: cross out 'Department of' and read what's left. That's your filing word.
Mnemonic: 'Drop the Department, Keep the Key word.' D→K. Focus on the unique identifier.
If it starts with 'Department/Bureau/Office/Commission' → find the distinctive word. File there.
STANDARD: The 'of WHAT?' technique: every government prefix ends with 'of' or 'on.' Answer the question 'of/on WHAT?' and you have your filing word. Department of Education → of WHAT? Education → E. Commission on Audit → on WHAT? Audit → A. Works every time without exception.

Visual metaphor: imagine a filing cabinet with 26 drawers. Government offices are 'assigned' to their distinctive-word drawer: Education goes in E, Health in H, Budget in B. They DON'T all squeeze into the D drawer. This image makes the distribution logic visceral and memorable.

Quick-reference for common departments: Budget→B, Education→E, Finance→F, Health→H, Interior→I, Justice→J, Labor→L, Science→S, Tourism→T, Trade→T. Memorize these specific mappings for exam speed — these are the most frequently tested agencies.

Contrast drill: write 10 department names. For each, write TWO positions: (1) where it files with distinctive-word rule (CSE standard), (2) where it files as-written. Practice until you can instantly produce both. The exam may ask for either depending on instructions.

Process automation: see 'Department of...' → brain immediately asks 'of WHAT?' → answer jumps to mind → note its first letter → done. This 3-second sequence should become reflexive. Practice on all Philippine government agencies you can name until the 'of WHAT?' response is automatic.
DETAILED: Build a government office quick-recall table: memorize the distinctive word AND its filing letter for the 15 most common Philippine agencies. Budget(B), Customs(C), Education(E), Environment(E), Finance(F), Health(H), Immigration(I), Interior(I), Internal Revenue(I), Justice(J), Labor(L), Public Works(P), Science(S), Tourism(T), Trade(T). Having these pre-loaded means zero processing time for familiar agencies on exam day.

The 'cross-out visualization' technique: when you see a government name, mentally draw a line through 'Department of' / 'Bureau of' / 'Office of.' What remains AFTER the line is visually prominent and becomes your filing key. This physical-mental action is faster than abstract 'rearrangement' because it's a subtraction (remove prefix) rather than a permutation (swap elements).

Disambiguation drill for same-letter distinctive words: Environment(E) vs Education(E) → both file under E, need position 2+ comparison: d(Education) vs n(Environment) → d<n → Education first. Internal Revenue(I) vs Immigration(I) → m(Immigration) vs n(Internal) → m<n → Immigration first. Interior(I) vs Immigration(I) → m(Immigration) vs n(Interior) → m<n → Immigration first. Practice these same-initial pairs specifically.

Instruction sensitivity training: Create practice questions with TWO versions — one with default instructions and one with 'file as written.' Answer both. For the default version, Department of Education → E. For the as-written version, Department of Education → D. Practice switching between modes until both feel equally natural. The exam's instruction override is rare but devastating if missed.

Integration mnemonic for TANG's G-rule with the full system: T(The→end)=surface edit, A(Acronyms)=no change, N(Numbers→words)=translation, G(Government→distinctive word)=rearrangement. The G-rule is the ONLY one requiring genuine word-order change. This makes it the hardest to automate and the one most deserving of dedicated practice. Allocate 40% of your business filing practice time to government office entries specifically.

sections.section_title: 4.5 Mixed Filing: Putting It All Together

SIMPLIFIED: Mixed filing means applying all four TANG rules to one list. Classify each entry, then alphabetize.
Step 1: identify type (company/number/acronym/government). Step 2: convert. Step 3: alphabetize.
The exam gives you mixed lists — companies, numbers, acronyms, government offices all together.
Key skill: quickly deciding WHICH rule applies to EACH entry before you start comparing.
After converting everything, just alphabetize normally by first filing unit. The hard part is the conversion.
STANDARD: Mixed filing combines all four TANG rules in a single alphabetized list. For each entry, you must: (1) classify its type (company, numeric, acronym, government office), (2) apply the appropriate transformation, and (3) determine the first filing unit. Only then can you alphabetize the entries using standard letter-by-letter comparison.

The entry types and their rules in one place: Company name → file as written (Globe Telecom → G). Company with 'The' → move 'The' to end (The Freeman → F). Numeric name → spell out (7-Eleven → S). Acronym → file letter by letter (CSC → C). Government office → distinctive word first (Dept of Education → E).

The cognitive challenge of mixed filing isn't the individual rules — each is simple. The challenge is applying DIFFERENT rules to DIFFERENT entries in the SAME list. You must switch between mental modes for each entry: 'This one's a company (as written), this one's a number (spell it), this one's government (distinctive word).'

After classification and conversion, mixed filing reduces to basic alphabetizing. Compare the first filing units of all converted entries, then order them A-Z. If two entries share the same first letter, compare position 2 and beyond using standard multi-letter comparison. All the basic alphabetizing skills still apply.

The TANG mnemonic serves as your classification checklist: scan each entry asking — starts with The? (T) Is it an acronym? (A) Contains a number? (N) Is it a government office? (G). The first match tells you which rule to apply. If none match, it's a standard company name filed as written.
DETAILED: Mixed filing is the synthesis skill that the CSE tests most heavily in business filing questions. It requires executing a multi-step process for each entry in a list: Step 1 (classification) — determine entry type. Step 2 (transformation) — apply TANG rule. Step 3 (extraction) — identify first filing unit. Step 4 (comparison) — alphabetize all entries by their filing units. Errors at any step cascade into wrong answers. The exam presents 4-5 mixed entries knowing that correct classification is the primary differentiator.

A complete mixed filing example: Given — Department of Science and Technology, 3M Philippines, The Philippine Star, NBI, Globe Telecom. Step 1: Government office, numeric name, company with The, acronym, company. Step 2: Science and Technology Dept of, Three M Philippines, Philippine Star (The), NBI, Globe Telecom. Step 3: Science(S), Three(T), Philippine(P), NBI(N), Globe(G). Step 4: Globe(G), NBI(N), Philippine(P), Science(S), Three(T). Every entry used a different rule.

Common mixed-filing error patterns: (1) Applying one rule to all entries (e.g., all as-written). (2) Applying the right rule to most but misclassifying one entry (e.g., treating an acronym as a government office because you know what it stands for). (3) Correct classification but incorrect alphabetizing of the converted forms (e.g., getting the conversion right but then comparing positions wrong). Each error type requires different prevention strategies.

The section demonstrates that after transformation, all entries participate equally in alphabetical comparison. A converted numeric name (Three M Philippines) competes for position against a converted government name (Science and Technology, Dept of) and a raw company name (Globe Telecom) using the same letter-by-letter rules. There's no hierarchy or precedence between entry types — they all file in one unified A-Z sequence.

Speed optimization for mixed filing: Process entries in order of complexity — acronyms first (no transformation needed, just note the letter), then companies (minimal processing), then The-names (quick move), then numbers (mental conversion), and finally government offices (rearrangement needed). This 'easy-to-hard' processing order builds momentum and ensures simple entries don't get slowed by complex-entry processing.

SIMPLIFIED: Globe(G), NBI(N), Philippine Star-The(P), Science-Dept(S), Three M(T). Five entries, four rules, one alphabetical list.
Mixed list: BSP(B), Jollibee(J), Philippine Daily Inquirer-The(P), Public Works-Dept(P), Seven-Eleven(S).
Quick example: COA(C) vs '7-Eleven'(Seven=S) vs Dept of Tourism(Tourism=T). Order: COA, Seven-Eleven, Tourism.
Company + government + acronym: Globe(G), Education-Dept(E), NBI(N). Order: Education, Globe, NBI.
Four TANG rules in one: The Freeman(F), 3M(Three=T), CSC(C), Dept of Health(Health=H). Order: CSC, Freeman, Health, Three M.
STANDARD: Full mixed example: Arrange — Dept of Public Works (DPWH), 7-Eleven, The Philippine Daily Inquirer, BSP, Jollibee Foods. Classify/convert: Public Works Dept(P), Seven-Eleven(S), Philippine Daily Inquirer The(P), BSP(B), Jollibee(J). First units: P, S, P, B, J. Order: BSP(B), Jollibee(J), Philippine Daily Inquirer(P-h), Public Works(P-u), Seven-Eleven(S).

Same-letter resolution in mixed lists: 'Philippine Star (The)' (P-h-i-l) vs 'PhilHealth' (P-h-i-l) vs 'Pag-IBIG' (P-a-g). Position 2: h, h, a. Since a<h, Pag-IBIG first. Between Philippine Star and PhilHealth: P-h-i-l-i-p vs P-h-i-l-H-e. Position 5: i vs H (=h). i>h? Actually i(9)>h(8). So PhilHealth before Philippine Star. Final: Pag-IBIG, PhilHealth, Philippine Star.

Government + acronym confusion: 'DENR' (acronym → D-E-N-R) vs 'Department of Education' (full name → Education = E). DENR files under D. Education files under E. D<E, so DENR comes first. Despite DENR standing for a department, it's GIVEN as an acronym — file it as one.

Numeric + government same-section scenario: '7-Eleven' (Seven=S) vs 'Department of Science and Technology' (Science=S) vs 'SSS' (S-S-S). All file under S! Position 2: a(San, if present), c(Science), e(Seven), S(SSS). For Science vs Seven: c<e → Science first. For Seven vs SSS: e<S → Seven first (since e<s). Order: Science and Technology Dept, Seven-Eleven, SSS.

Real exam arrangement: Dept of Tourism, The Manila Hotel, NBI, 3M Philippines, Globe Telecom. Convert: Tourism Dept(T), Manila Hotel The(M), NBI(N), Three M(T), Globe(G). First letters: T, M, N, T, G. Order: Globe(G), Manila Hotel(M), NBI(N), Three M(T-h), Tourism(T-o). Note: Three(T-h-r) vs Tourism(T-o-u) — h<o, so Three M before Tourism.
DETAILED: Complete 5-entry walkthrough: Arrange — PhilHealth, Pag-IBIG, Dept of Environment and Natural Resources, 8th Avenue Restaurant, The Freeman. Step 1: Classify — mixed-case acronym, hyphenated acronym, government office, numeric name, company with The. Step 2: Convert — PhilHealth(P-h), PagIBIG(P-a), Environment Dept(E-n), Eighth Avenue(E-i), Freeman The(F-r). Step 3: First letters — P, P, E, E, F. Step 4: Resolve E-group first: Eighth(E-i) vs Environment(E-n). i<n → Eighth first. Then F. Then P-group: PagIBIG(P-a) vs PhilHealth(P-h). a<h → PagIBIG first. Final: 8th Avenue Restaurant, Dept of Environment, The Freeman, Pag-IBIG, PhilHealth.

Tricky mixed comparison: COA vs CSC vs Coca-Cola Philippines. COA(C-O-A) = acronym. CSC(C-S-C) = acronym. Coca-Cola(C-o-c-a) = company (hyphen ignored). All start with C. Position 2: O(COA), S(CSC), o(Coca-Cola). Case-insensitive: o=O. So COA and Coca-Cola both have 'o' at position 2, CSC has 'S.' Since o<s, both COA and Coca-Cola come before CSC. Between COA and Coca-Cola: position 3 — A(COA) vs c(Coca-Cola). A vs c (case-insensitive: a vs c). a<c. So COA first. Final: COA, Coca-Cola Philippines, CSC.

Maximum complexity scenario: Arrange — GSIS, Dept of Justice, 24/7 Express, The Philippine Star, Bank of the Philippine Islands, Globe Telecom. Classify: acronym, government, numeric, company-The, company, company. Convert: GSIS(G-S), Justice Dept(J-u), Twentyfour Seven Express(T-w), Philippine Star The(P-h), Bank of the Philippine Islands(B-a), Globe Telecom(G-l). First letters: G, J, T, P, B, G. Order: Bank(B), Globe(G-l), GSIS(G-S), Justice(J), Philippine Star(P), Twentyfour Seven(T). Note: Globe(G-l) before GSIS(G-S) because l<s.

The 'same organization, different form' scenario: List contains both 'DOH' and 'Department of Health.' DOH(acronym) = D-O-H. Department of Health(government) = Health, Dept of = H. These file in DIFFERENT sections (D vs H). If both appear in the same list, they're treated as different entries with different filing positions. DOH goes between DENR and DILG. Health goes between Globe and Interior. This is correct per filing rules.

Speed technique demonstration: Given 5 entries, process in complexity order. (1) Acronyms first — NBI=N, done. CSC=C, done. (2) Companies — Globe=G, done. (3) Numbers — 7-Eleven=Seven=S, done. (4) Government — Dept of Tourism=Tourism=T, done. Now sort: C, G, N, S, T → CSC, Globe, NBI, Seven-Eleven, Tourism. Total processing: classification (10s) + noting letters (5s) + ordering (5s) = 20 seconds. The easy-to-hard processing order prevents cognitive overload.

SIMPLIFIED: Mixed filing = classify each entry, apply its rule, then alphabetize all the results together.
TANG tells you the rule. Basic alphabetizing does the rest. Two skills combined.
The exam's main test: can you apply DIFFERENT rules to DIFFERENT entries in ONE list?
After conversion, everything competes equally in A-Z. No entry type has priority over another.
Process: (1) classify, (2) convert, (3) note first letter, (4) alphabetize. Four steps, every time.
STANDARD: Mixed filing is the synthesis of all TANG rules applied to a single list. Each entry gets classified and transformed independently, then all transformed entries are alphabetized together using standard letter-by-letter comparison. The challenge is correct classification — individual rules are simple.

After transformation, entry types lose their identity. A converted numeric name, a rearranged government name, and a raw company name all compete equally in the same A-Z sequence. There's no separate section for acronyms or numbers. Everything files in one unified alphabet.

The four-step process: (1) Scan entries and classify each by type. (2) Apply TANG transformation to each. (3) Extract first filing unit from each converted entry. (4) Alphabetize by first units (and further positions if needed). Errors at step 1 produce wrong answers regardless of how well you execute steps 2-4.

Key insight: mixed filing difficulty scales with the NUMBER of different rules needed per list. A list of 5 companies = easy (one rule repeated). A list with one company, one acronym, one number, one government office, and one The-name = hard (five different rules). The exam targets the hard case.

Speed technique: process entries in complexity order. Acronyms first (no conversion = instant). Companies next (minimal processing). Then The-names, then numbers, then government offices last (most complex). This reduces cognitive switching costs and builds momentum from easy to hard.
DETAILED: Mixed filing represents the full business filing skill: classification + transformation + comparison applied to heterogeneous entry sets. The section demonstrates that the TANG rules, when applied correctly to each entry, reduce any mixed list to a standard alphabetizing problem. The 'mixed' difficulty is entirely in the classification-transformation phase — once entries are in their filing form, comparison uses the same basic alphabetizing techniques from earlier lessons.

The process has four distinct cognitive phases: Phase 1 (Classification) — identify entry type for each item. This requires pattern recognition: all-caps=acronym, digits=numeric, 'Department/Bureau'=government, 'The'+name=The-rule, else=company. Phase 2 (Transformation) — apply the corresponding TANG rule. Phase 3 (Extraction) — identify the first filing unit of each transformed entry. Phase 4 (Ordering) — standard alphabetical comparison of first units, then subsequent positions if needed.

Error analysis for mixed filing: Type 1 errors (misclassification) — applying wrong rule to an entry. These produce consistently wrong positions. Type 2 errors (conversion mistakes) — e.g., spelling a number wrong. These produce slightly wrong positions. Type 3 errors (comparison mistakes) — alphabetizing the correctly-converted entries incorrectly. Type 1 is most common and most damaging because one misclassification displaces an entry by multiple positions.

The integration principle: after transformation, all entries participate in ONE unified alphabet. A government office filed under its distinctive word competes with companies, acronyms, and numeric names at whatever letter it lands on. 'Education, Department of' at position E competes with 'Eight Avenue' (numeric→Eighth) also at position E. The system's elegance is that different rules feed into one common comparison framework.

Mixed filing as exam skill: The CSE presents this as the ultimate test of business filing competence. A student who can handle mixed lists has demonstrated: (1) rule knowledge (knowing all four TANG rules), (2) classification ability (matching entries to rules), (3) conversion accuracy (applying rules correctly), and (4) alphabetizing skill (ordering the results). All four components must work together for a correct answer. This is why mixed filing questions are the highest-difficulty items in the Clerical Ability business filing subset.

SIMPLIFIED: CSE Sub-Professional (165 items, 2h40m, 80% passing) — mixed lists are the most common business filing format.
The exam always mixes entry types. You MUST classify before comparing. No shortcut around it.
Budget 40-50 seconds for mixed filing items. Classification takes the most time.
Trap: applying one rule to all entries. Each entry needs its OWN rule based on its type.
Sub-Professional Clerical Ability: master TANG classification and these become reliable points.
STANDARD: In the CSE Sub-Professional (165 items, 2h40m, 80% passing), mixed filing questions are the standard format for business filing items. Expect 4-5 entries of varied types requiring you to apply multiple TANG rules in one question. This tests both rule knowledge and classification speed.

For the CSE (Sub-Professional, 165 items, 2h40m, 80% to pass), mixed filing items take 40-50 seconds. The time breakdown: classification (15s), conversion (10s), ordering (15-20s). Practice should target each phase separately, then integrate for speed.

CSE strategy (Sub-Professional, 165 items, 2h40m, 80% passing): After classifying and converting all entries, write down (mentally or on scratch paper) just the first filing LETTER of each entry. Then sort those letters. This separates the complex work (classification/conversion) from the simple work (alphabetizing letters).

The CSE Sub-Professional (165 items, 2h40m, 80% passing) uses distractor answers that result from common misclassification. One distractor has the government office under D. Another has the numeric entry at the start. A third has the acronym expanded. Recognizing these distractor patterns helps verify your answer.

For the CSE Sub-Professional Clerical Ability section (165 items, 2h40m, 80% passing): Mixed filing is the culmination skill. If you can handle mixed lists consistently, you can handle any business filing question the exam presents. Make this your primary practice format for the last week before the exam.
DETAILED: The CSE Sub-Professional (165 items, 2h40m, 80% passing) designs mixed filing questions to test multi-rule competence. A typical question presents 5 entries: 1 government office, 1 acronym, 1 numeric name, 1 The-company, and 1 regular company. This ensures all four TANG rules are needed in one item. The exam's answer choices are constructed so that each common error type produces a different wrong answer — making it possible to diagnose the mistake from the wrong choice selected.

Time management for CSE Sub-Professional (165 items, 2h40m, 80% passing): Mixed filing items are 'high-investment, high-return' — they take more time (40-50 seconds) but reward systematic work with definitive correct answers. Unlike ambiguous questions in other sections, business filing has ONE correct answer determined by rules. Every second invested in correct classification pays off in guaranteed accuracy.

Exam preparation strategy for CSE Sub-Professional (165 items, 2h40m, 80% to pass): Practice mixed filing in three phases. Phase 1 (Days 1-5): Practice classification only — see 20 entries, identify all types in 30 seconds. Phase 2 (Days 6-10): Practice full conversion — classify AND transform 20 entries in 60 seconds. Phase 3 (Days 11-14): Full mixed filing problems under exam time pressure — 5-entry questions in 45 seconds each. This progressive skill-building ensures each component is solid before integration.

For the CSE Sub-Professional (165 items, 2h40m, 80% passing): Mixed filing questions have a 'verification trick' — after selecting your answer, check if any entry is filed in a position that violates its type's rule. Is a government office clustered with other D-entries? Wrong. Is a numeric entry before A? Wrong. Is an acronym in its expanded-name position? Wrong. These quick checks catch errors before you finalize.

Strategic insight for CSE Sub-Professional (165 items, 2h40m, 80% passing): The exam's mixed filing items are among the most PREDICTABLE in the entire test. They follow a rigid structure: present mixed entries → require TANG classification → produce one deterministic correct order. Unlike reading comprehension or analytical items that require interpretation, business filing is purely procedural. A student who has automated TANG classification will get these correct EVERY time. This predictability makes them the highest-reliability scoring opportunity in Clerical Ability.

SIMPLIFIED: TANG checklist for each entry: The? Acronym? Number? Government? Apply the first match.
After TANG conversion, just note the first LETTER of each entry. Sort those letters. Done.
Process each entry separately, then combine. Don't try to compare BEFORE converting.
Mental flow: see entry → classify (2 sec) → convert (3 sec) → note letter (1 sec). Repeat for each.
Mixed filing = TANG + basic alphabetizing. Two skills you already know, combined.
STANDARD: The TANG classification sequence: For each entry, run through T-A-N-G in order. First match = your rule. Starts with 'The'? → T-rule. All caps/acronym? → A-rule. Has digits? → N-rule. Starts with Department/Bureau/Office? → G-rule. No match? → file as written. This sequence takes 2-3 seconds per entry.

Two-pass technique for mixed lists: Pass 1 — classify and convert each entry, writing just the first filing letter. Pass 2 — sort the letters alphabetically. This separates the hard work (classification) from the easy work (ordering). Each pass uses a different cognitive skill without interference.

Exam-day checklist after answering a mixed filing question: (1) Is any government office under D/B/O? → probably wrong. (2) Is any numeric entry before A-entries? → probably wrong. (3) Are any acronyms in their expanded position? → probably wrong. If all three checks pass, your answer is likely correct.

Practice format: create 10 mixed-entry cards (5 entries each). Time yourself classifying all 5 entries, converting them, and ordering them. Target: 40 seconds per card. Track which entry TYPE causes the most hesitation — that's your weak point for focused practice.

Integration mantra: 'Type first, rule second, letter third, order last.' Four steps, always in this sequence. Never jump to ordering before classification is complete. Never compare entries before conversion is done. The sequence prevents the cascading errors that wrong classification causes.
DETAILED: Build a 'rapid classification flowchart' for exam-day mental use: ENTRY → All caps, 2-5 letters? → YES = acronym (file as-is). NO → Starts with a digit? → YES = number (spell out). NO → Starts with 'The'? → YES = move The to end. NO → Starts with Dept/Bureau/Office/Commission? → YES = distinctive word first. NO → file as written. This binary decision tree takes max 4 decisions (10 seconds) for any entry. With practice, most entries resolve at decision 1 or 2 (5 seconds).

The 'letter extraction table' technique: for each entry in the question, immediately write (mentally) a small table: Entry | Type | Filing Letter. Fill this table before attempting any ordering. Example: Globe=Company=G, NBI=Acronym=N, 7-Eleven=Number=S, Dept of Tourism=Gov=T, The Manila Hotel=The-company=M. Now your ordering problem is just: G, N, S, T, M → alphabetize: G, M, N, S, T. This decomposition makes complex problems trivial.

Error prevention protocol: After determining your answer, apply three verification rules. Rule 1: no government office should be adjacent to other same-prefix offices (they should be scattered). Rule 2: no numeric entry should precede all letter entries (it should be within A-Z). Rule 3: no acronym should be in its expanded-form position. These three rules catch the three most common TANG-rule violations in under 10 seconds.

Progressive speed drill schedule: Week 1 — 5-entry mixed problems in 60 seconds (learning). Week 2 — same in 45 seconds (building speed). Week 3 — same in 35 seconds (approaching exam speed). Week 4 — 30 seconds (exam-ready). Track accuracy at each speed level. If accuracy drops below 90% at a given speed, slow down and rebuild. Speed without accuracy is worthless on the CSE.

The 'type tagging' exam technique: as you read each entry in a question, immediately tag it mentally: [C] for company, [A] for acronym, [N] for number, [G] for government, [T] for The-name. Then process each tag group separately: [A] entries need no conversion (instant letters). [C] entries need minimal processing. [T] entries need The-removal. [N] entries need spelling. [G] entries need rearrangement. Processing by group reduces cognitive switching costs compared to processing entries in the order they appear.
